subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In Lorenz's research, what did the goslings do shortly after hatching?
options: Sought contact comfort from a cloth surrogate
Imprinted on the first moving object they saw
questions.explain: Lorenz found goslings imprinted on the first large moving object they encountered after hatching, often Lorenz himself.

questions.q: What did Schaffer and Emerson find regarding the formation of multiple attachments?
options: Infants never form attachments to more than one person
By one year, most infants had formed multiple attachments
Multiple attachments only formed in institutionalised children
Multiple attachments formed before specific attachments
questions.explain: By around one year of age the majority of infants in the study had developed multiple attachments to several people.

questions.q: An infant classified as 'insecure-resistant' (Type C) typically shows:
options: High anxiety, distress on separation, and resistance to comfort at reunion
Indifference to the caregiver and willingness to explore
questions.explain: Type C infants show intense distress and seek yet resist comfort (e.g. pushing the caregiver away) at reunion.

questions.q: Bowlby's 'social releasers' are best described as:
options: Behaviours measured in the Strange Situation
Innate behaviours such as smiling and cooing that elicit caregiving
questions.explain: Social releasers are innate infant behaviours like smiling that trigger an adult caregiving response and promote attachment.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's original sample, which attachment type was the most common?
questions.explain: Secure attachment (Type B) was the most common classification, found in around two-thirds of infants.

questions.q: What were the long-term effects on Harlow's maternally deprived monkeys?
options: They formed secure attachments to the wire mother
They showed social and emotional disturbance and poor parenting in adulthood
They developed normally once reintroduced to peers
questions.explain: Harlow's deprived monkeys grew into socially and sexually abnormal adults who were often neglectful or aggressive parents.

questions.q: Zeanah et al.'s Bucharest Early Intervention study found that institutionalised children most often showed which attachment type?
questions.explain: In the Bucharest study a high proportion of institutionalised children were classified as disorganised in attachment.

questions.q: In Bowlby's monotropic theory, what does the 'internal working model' provide?
options: A timetable for the stages of attachment
A biological clock determining the critical period
A mental template for future relationships based on the first attachment
questions.explain: The internal working model is a cognitive template, formed from the primary attachment, that shapes expectations of later relationships.

questions.q: In van IJzendoorn's meta-analysis, where was insecure-resistant attachment notably higher and insecure-avoidant lower?
questions.explain: Collectivist samples such as Japan and Israel showed higher rates of resistant and lower rates of avoidant attachment.

questions.q: Meltzoff and Moore (1977) are best known for research demonstrating which phenomenon in infants as young as two to three weeks old?
questions.explain: Meltzoff and Moore observed that infants appeared to imitate adult facial and hand gestures, providing evidence for early interactional synchrony.

questions.q: Bowlby's 'law of continuity' states that:
options: The more constant and predictable a child's care, the better the attachment quality
Attachment is continuous across all caregivers
questions.explain: The law of continuity states that consistent, predictable care leads to better-quality attachment.

questions.q: In Harlow's monkey studies, what did the infant monkeys prefer when frightened?
options: The mother offering the most food regardless of texture
The cloth-covered mother that provided contact comfort
The wire mother that dispensed food
questions.explain: Harlow found frightened monkeys clung to the soft cloth mother for comfort, showing contact comfort mattered more than food.

questions.q: Rutter distinguished maternal 'deprivation' from 'privation', where privation means:
options: The failure to ever form an attachment in the first place
The loss of the internal working model
Temporary separation from an existing attachment figure
questions.explain: Privation is the failure to form any attachment, which Rutter argued is more damaging than deprivation (loss of an existing one).

questions.q: In Schaffer and Emerson's (1964) Glasgow study, at roughly what age did most infants form their first specific attachment?
questions.explain: Schaffer and Emerson found that specific attachments typically formed at around seven months, shown by separation and stranger anxiety.

questions.q: What did Lorenz conclude about imprinting and timing?
options: Imprinting only occurs after the first month
Imprinting must occur within a critical period or it will not occur at all
Imprinting can occur at any point in life
questions.explain: Lorenz argued imprinting must take place within a fixed critical period, after which it would not happen.

questions.q: Harlow's findings most directly challenge which explanation of attachment?
options: The concept of a critical period
questions.explain: By showing comfort outweighed food, Harlow undermined the learning theory idea that attachment forms through association with feeding.

questions.q: Which of the following is a methodological weakness of using animal studies (Lorenz, Harlow) to explain human attachment?
options: Findings may not generalise from animals to humans due to differences in cognition and behaviour
They cannot establish cause and effect
questions.explain: A key limitation is reduced generalisability, as humans differ from geese and monkeys in cognitive and emotional complexity.

questions.q: Bowlby's maternal deprivation hypothesis argues that prolonged separation in early life can lead to:
questions.explain: Bowlby linked maternal deprivation to affectionless psychopathy and low IQ, as suggested by his 44 thieves study.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, what is the procedure primarily designed to measure?
options: The quality or type of attachment
The strength of the internal working model directly
questions.explain: The Strange Situation is a controlled observation designed to assess the type or quality of an infant's attachment.

questions.q: According to learning theory, how is attachment explained through classical conditioning?
options: The infant imprints on the caregiver during a critical period
The infant is positively reinforced by the removal of discomfort
An internal working model forms a template for relationships
The caregiver (neutral stimulus) becomes associated with food (unconditioned stimulus) to produce pleasure
questions.explain: In classical conditioning the caregiver becomes a conditioned stimulus by being repeatedly paired with the pleasure of food.

questions.q: In Bowlby's theory, what is meant by 'monotropy'?
options: The tendency to imprint on the first moving object
A learned association between caregiver and food
A special, primary attachment to one particular caregiver
questions.explain: Monotropy refers to the infant's single, primary attachment to one main figure, which Bowlby saw as the most important.

questions.q: Research on the role of the father (e.g. Grossmann, 2002) suggests fathers' attachments are particularly associated with which type of behaviour?
questions.explain: Grossmann's longitudinal research suggested fathers' role relates more to play and stimulation than to nurturing care.

questions.q: A characteristic effect of institutionalisation reported in Romanian orphan studies is:
options: Reduced stranger anxiety in adulthood only
questions.explain: Disinhibited attachment, marked by indiscriminate affection towards strangers, was a common effect of institutional care.

questions.q: A strength of Schaffer and Emerson's study is that observations were made in:
options: The infants' own homes by parents, giving high ecological validity
A controlled laboratory using the Strange Situation
questions.explain: Data were gathered in the family home through parental reports, giving the findings high ecological validity.

questions.q: According to Schaffer and Emerson's stages of attachment, which stage comes immediately before specific attachment?
questions.explain: The order is asocial, indiscriminate, specific, then multiple attachments, so indiscriminate attachment precedes specific attachment.

questions.q: Hazan and Shaver's (1987) 'Love Quiz' study supported continuity by finding that:
options: Avoidant infants always became secure adults
Childhood attachment had no link to adult love
Adult romantic attachment styles correlated with reported infant attachment types
Attachment type changes randomly in adulthood
questions.explain: Hazan and Shaver found correlations between recalled childhood attachment and the way participants experienced adult romantic love.

questions.q: Securely attached infants tend, on average, to go on to have:
options: More friendships and better-quality adult relationships
No measurable difference in later relationships
questions.explain: Research links secure infant attachment with more successful friendships and adult relationships via a positive internal working model.

questions.q: Which behaviours did the Strange Situation assess?
options: Proximity-seeking, exploration/secure-base, stranger anxiety, separation anxiety and reunion behaviour
questions.explain: Ainsworth recorded proximity-seeking, secure-base exploration, stranger anxiety, separation anxiety and reunion behaviour.

questions.q: What is meant by 'interactional synchrony'?
options: The caregiver and infant mirroring each other's actions and emotions in a coordinated, simultaneous way
The infant developing a routine of feeding times
The caregiver and infant taking turns to respond alternately
The infant showing distress on separation from the caregiver
questions.explain: Interactional synchrony is the simultaneous, coordinated mirroring of actions and emotions between caregiver and infant.

questions.q: How does operant conditioning explain attachment via negative reinforcement of the caregiver?
options: Crying is reduced when the caregiver responds, reinforcing caregiving behaviour
The caregiver feeds the infant to gain food rewards
The infant associates the caregiver with food
The infant imprints to avoid punishment
questions.explain: The caregiver is negatively reinforced because responding to the infant stops the aversive crying, increasing caregiving behaviour.
